searchText: Can someone point me to the priority fee for each block and the current priority fee? Worked all day and I am trying to catch up on all the news and stats. Do you mean base fee, <@!604977744044097546> ? priority fee is set by each txn https://watchtheburn.com/ has good data my hashrate is way diwn down <@!552133098075193354> no, looking for priority fee data. I can figure out the priority fee from total reward minus block reward minus MEV, but was looking for something that shows the priority fee per block either in a table or on a chart. I see that the priority fee is probably larger than it will be in a week or 2 once the wallets implement a 1559 specific interface. I am looking to track the change. Oh cool watch the burn is back up now, though it appears to still be a bit slow, not working at all. Transaction receipt has an `effectiveGasPrice` field IIRC. You can subtract the base fee for the block from that to get the effective priority fee. This chart is quite nice: https://dune.xyz/queries/97532/196164 https://etherchain.org/api/gasPriceOracle supports 1559 now Compare to: Actually looks pretty close! How is this organic simulation done? Just wanted to understand what I'm seeing here I think the script was something like: ``` for i in range(2000): if random.random() < 0.5: txpool += 1 if random.random() < 0.01: block_sizes.append(min(txpool, 100)) txpool -= min(txpool, 100) ``` Why is setting 97 maxfee when basefee is 48 a good idea? As per this API You get refunded on excess max fee. Premium is the one you don't get a refund on. Yup am aware but even so Setting your max fee to 2x the current basefee is good rule of thumb for achieving almost certain inclusion. As Micah says the refund excess gets refunded. In principle you you set your max fee to the largest amount you are willing to pay for instant transaction inclusion. But using 2x is good default. Why should users want certain inclusion in the next block? Imo the average use case is simple transfers or uniswap trades. Uniswap traders imo can execute trades more cheaply if they're more patient and willing to eat failed tx fees. (cause cost of failed tx is much smaller than cost of successful tx) And simple transfers are not gonna fail anyway so there's even less hurry Basically even the "Slow" bid feels like overbidding to me For the novice user, their *expectation* is that things happen right away. This allows us to provide that expected behavior to the novice user. A more advanced user may want to do things to try to time their inclusion based on seasonality of gas prices, but that is definitely an advanced behavior (which you can still do). Considering how expensive how L1 is, shouldn't we instead teach users to be patient and execute more cheaply Rather than letting them do what they already expect to do for more expensive Atleast in "Slow" bid <@!301186049323958275> I think the way to get a really great experience would be to include an "expiry" field in the transaction header (transactions are invalid in blocks after expiry) and have interfaces default to sending: Max Fee = 2 x Current Base Fee, Priority Fee = 1 GWei, Expiry = 1 min. Then apps just get to show a timer and users are promised that either their transaction succeeded or failed for free (and they can just retry without issues). This has potential to open up some DoS vectors that we would need to analyze and deal with. I personally don't think UX should be a priority for ethereum upgrades. And DOS protection layers like flashbots will make things better anyway (no cost to failed tx). I think the expiry expression could be on the wallet side. You sign a low fee transaction for your wallet, signal that it is for 24 hours. The wallet holds the transaction on their server, and broadcasts if it becomes viable. If it never becomes viable, the mempool never sees it. Yup then the wallet server is the DOS protection layer. Same thing :) I would have expected a different behavior from the wallet: you sign your transaction and secretly the wallet makes you sign another one cancellimg And after some time it sends it if the first one didn't get included Could it fall under the JSON-RPC? `eth_sendDelayedTransaction`, where the parameters are the same for `eth_sendTransaction`, but there is another field `sendIfBaseFee:<baseFeePerGas QUANTITY>` and then the signed message can be passed to any service that holds and broadcasts (e.g. the wallet, or some local process, or another provider) I see your point. It is fee to sign 10 different transactions and have the wallet deal with the transmission. Is there value in standardising the pattern? is there anything different in spending gas efficiently now, should we just use the default metamask gas estimate or should we be adjusting? The default will be fine. It may save you some money if your Metamask has received the upgrade they are rolling out gradually over the next few days/week. They made a video to help outline the new interface https://metamask.io/1559.html#1559-video Thanks
